articles.summary: Directory of display and professional advertisements in columns 1-4 of page 1.

articles.text: Newspapers are rejoicing over the almost certain reduction of second class postage from two cents to one per pound.
articles.summary: Notes the expected cut in second-class postage.

articles.text: To-day, the Cow Boy is one year old. It is a pretty healthy infant and we hope will grow rapidly with its increasing years.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy marks its first anniversary.

articles.text: The bills for the removal of the capitol in both the house and council have been "gently but firmly squashed." South as well as north, Dakotains realize that nothing is to be gained by opening the question. Bismarck is and well be the capitol.
articles.summary: Reports defeat of the territorial capital-removal bills; Bismarck remains the capital.

articles.text: We wish to say a word to every reader of the Cow Boy. A spirit of criticism never has and never can advance any business interest. When a man sees that another is wrong, how much better it would be to go to him and explain his mistake, than to go to another man and criticise him for his unintentional error. Many illustrations of this point have come under our notice, and we hope in the future that our citizens will advise rather than criticise, look on the bright side and not on the dark.
articles.summary: Urges Medora citizens to advise rather than criticise one another.

articles.text: All over the country, there is a determined cutting of rates by railroads and and transportation lines. Rates from St. Paul to Portland will be greatly reduced and rates, especially to emigrants, will be brought so low by the Northern Pacific that northern Dakota can compete with southern Dokota in giving cheap homes to settlers. The "war is carried into Africa" by trans-Atlantic lines and through tickets can now be bought from Liverpool to Chicago for eleven dollars. The result will be that vast numbers of settlers will settle in the northwest this summer.
articles.summary: Railroad and steamship rate cutting expected to bring many settlers to the northwest.

articles.text: On and after the next issue of the Cow Boy the price of cattle brands will be reduced to $15 per year. This includes the whole cost, no extras whatever being charged. By reference to the rates of other cattle papers, it will be seen that the new rates are lower than any other. Our cuts are also larger and better than those of any other cattle paper published in the United States. We make this change in rates to meet outside competion alone, as we do not consider that our brand columns at present any more than pay for the space they occupy. Of course, every cattle man in the Bad Lands realizes that his brand in the Cow Boy is more valuable than in an outside paper, but we intend that the rates shall be no higher in the Cow Boy. The time of those who have paid in advance for next year will be extended in proportion to the reduction. By this move we expect to get every brand on the river and we can then, more than formerly, merit the patronage of the cattle men of the Bad Lands especially.
articles.summary: Announces brand advertisements will drop to $15 a year from the next issue.

articles.text: A check will be put upon shipping Texas cattle east and north by the railroads refusing to carry them until the responsibility for the spread of Texas fever has been placed. For instance, if a bunch of Texans are shipped east, and the same cars used afterward for domestic cattle, and the latter catch the fever, who is responsible? The railroads, or the owners of the Texans? During frosty weather there is no danger of the fever, but in warm weather it would seem that the only safe way would lie in a strict quarantine. For Texans shipped into Dakota, it might be a good plan to set off a portion of the Sioux reservation as a quarantine ground. Something of the kind must certainly be done, as a single herd of cattle infected with the disease might scatter its seeds through every herd on the river. For this reason it might be better for our association to call an earlier meeting than the annual one in April, as before then the frost will have disappeared and serious damage may be done. It is a good point for our cattle men to ponder.
articles.summary: Urges quarantine against Texas fever and suggests the stock association meet before its April annual meeting.

articles.headline: Admission and Division.
articles.text: We think there is scarcely a paper in the United States that has not expressed its views on the admission and division of Dakota. All, so far as we have seen, favor admission, but there is justly a difference of opinion on division. And well there may be, for we do not believe there is a private citizen of Dakota that way down in his heart wants our territory divided. The cry was first raised and is now kept alive by a set of pot-house politicians, whose only hope of making a living is in feeling on public pap, and a press bribed and bullied into obeying their masters, the politicians. The reasons for division all group into one, that the people of north and south Dakota cannot live together in harmony. This is as baseless a slander and as unmitigated a lie as could be perpetrated upon Dakota's citizens. The politicians of north and south Dakota, of course, cannot live together in harmony, because their future bread and butter depends on their present wrangling. Undivided, we can in time become one of the greatest states in the Union. Divided, we will ever occupy a middle plane. As every one knows, Dakota's politics have been and are now run by a close corporations of rascals who should, nearly every one, be behind the bars repenting of their sins, or more likely breeding new schemes of iniquity to hatch out on their release. It is time for the press of Dakota to come forth from bondage and pro[claim?] the voice of the people and not that of the politicians.
articles.summary: Editorial favoring Dakota's admission as one state and attacking the movement to divide the territory.

articles.headline: Stock Notes. Estrayed.
articles.text: From M. S. & F. Co., October 5, one sorrel horse; four white feet, white stripe in face, branded -Y- on left shoulder and [box brand] on left thigh. A reward of $25 will be paid for information leading to his recovery.
articles.summary: Estray notice from the Medora Stage and Forwarding Co. for a sorrel horse, $25 reward.

articles.headline: Strayed or Stolen.
articles.text:
From my ranch on Little Missouri, ten miles south of Medora, the night of November 19, a dark sorrel mare, weighing about nine hundred pounds, left front knee stiff, white and red scar on left side, far back, brand M bar on left hip. Mare about nine years old. The finder will be paid for his trouble by leaving information leading to her recovery with me.

A. Young, Medora, Dak.
articles.summary: A. Young seeks a dark sorrel mare lost from his ranch south of Medora.

articles.headline: Strayed or Stolen.
articles.text: From Little Missouri, July 6, 1884, a bay horse, eight years old and weighing about 1,000 pounds. The horse was branded with an anchor on left cheek and a hat brand on left shoulder. On the left hip he had a Texas brand, looking something like 7N, connected with flourish at top of N. A reward of $25 will be paid for information leading to his recovery. The horse is the property of John Pohl, and information can be brought or sent to the Cow Boy office.
articles.summary: Notice of John Pohl's bay horse lost from Little Missouri, $25 reward.

articles.headline: $50 Reward.
articles.text:
The above reward will be paid for the return of the following stock or a proportionate reward will be paid for the return of any of them. The stock consists of the following horses:

One bay mare, one brown mare and one roan mare, all young and branded double or reverse P on left shoulder as advertised in our brand columns. Also one light sorrel pony, white legs and face and branded NC on left shoulder and triangle JP on right shoulder also as advertised in our brand columns.

Gregor Lang, Medora, Dak.
articles.summary: Gregor Lang offers $50 for the return of three mares and a pony.

articles.text: The Colorado stock Grower's association has a record of thenty-two horse and cattle thieves convicted at an average cost of $70 each. Cheap riddance.
articles.summary: Colorado stock growers' record of convicting thieves.

articles.text: The Helena and Miles City stock organizations have merged into one, to be known as the "Montana Stock Growing Association." The spring meetings are to be held in Miles City and the fall meetings in Helena. The success of the Cheyenne association has conclusively proven that it is better to merge all smaller associations into a larger or at least have them subordiate to larger. More concerted and far more energetic action is possible under this system and we wish every success to the new association.
articles.summary: Helena and Miles City stock associations merge as the Montana Stock Growing Association.

articles.text: Although Medora has never been the scene, in spite of all reports to the contrary, of a six-shooter row among cow boys, we cannot help but join with other cattle papers in urging the necessity of discarding the six-shooters while in town, On the range, one sometimes is needed, but in town there is never any use for them. To carry a six-shooter should be "a custom more honored in the breach than the observance." A determined and united movement is being made among southern cattle men to stop the custom, and northern men are falling into line. The six-shooter is the one thing that gives cow boys a bad name, and we hope its days are numbered.
articles.summary: Urges cowboys to stop carrying six-shooters in town.

articles.text: From the oldest settlers and from weather reports we gather the fact that this winter so far has been the coldest that was ever experienced in the west. Notwithstanding this fact, cattle have never done better and were never in better condition at this season of the year. These facts are not stated as guess work but are the substanse of a large number of conversations. We must conclude then, that cold, especially where there is as good protection as there is in the Bad Lands has but little effect on the cattle. The snow is also deeper than for many years and in many places has crusted, but from all reliable sources we glean the fact that not over three per cent. of cattle will have died in the Bad Lands by spring and not over five per cent. in Montana.
articles.summary: Reports the coldest winter on record in the west but cattle in excellent condition, with losses expected under three per cent in the Bad Lands.

articles.text: From several reliable sources, comes the information that polled or hornless cattle are surely pushing themselves into favor as range cattle. Mr. L. C. Le Moyne, of the Le Moyne cattle Co. although an ardent admirer and extensive breeder of short-horn cattle, while here last summer expressed his firm belief that Polled-Angus bulls would be the future favorites and that polled cattle would be the most profitable for the range. Now comes the evidence of T. C. Power & Bro., who, according to the Stock Growers' Journal, have made careful tests as between Durham and Polled-Angus bulls and the result is that the latter are invariably the best rustlers, that they stay on the range longer, that they stand the cold better and that they are getting fat on the range while the Durhams are shivering about the corralls and finally that the Polled-Angus is "boss of the range." There are many good reasons for the superiority of Polled-Angus, the most important probably bring that all nourishment that goes to the horn in others cattle, goes to bone and meat in polled cattle and that the numerous diseases and accidents happening to horns are absent.
articles.summary: Polled-Angus cattle gaining favor on the range; cites L. C. Le Moyne and T. C. Power & Bro.

articles.text: The evidence now seems to be good that the foot and mouth disease has been thoroughly eradicated in England. If so, it is owing entirely to the action of the English government in appointing commissioners with full power to do any and all things toward destroying the disease. With such an example before us, it seems that before the periodical scares in reference to pleuro-pneumonia and Texas fever again arise, our government should appoint commissioners whose sole duty it shall be to attend to such diseases and prevent their spread. This is another good point for discussion by cattle organizations.
articles.summary: Urges federal commissioners to control cattle diseases, citing England's eradication of foot and mouth disease.

articles.text: A beautiful cow girl lives near Murkel County, Neb. She owns some stock, which she personally looks after. At a late round-up, her dazzling beauty and graceful horsemanship were wonderful to behold. A yearling broke from the herd which three cowboys failed to confine, when the beautiful girl dashed out after it, roping it on the second circle and pulled it by the horn of her saddle into the herd. The boys shouted, wept and never ceased to love. John Sergeant, of Montrose County, it may be added to this, has a 15-year old daughter, Miss Nellie, who has been bred in the saddle, and is accustomed to ride with her father all over his range. In addition to the young lady's graceful horsemanship, she can handle a lariat and branding-iron, and can ride a bucking horse with as much skill and grace as any cow boy that has been on the range since boyhood. Nellie Sergeant is dowered by her father with one-third of the increase of his herd, and when she chooses to marry, her husband will be a cattle king.—[Omaha Bee.
articles.summary: Clipped item from the Omaha Bee about cowgirls in Nebraska and Montrose County.

articles.text: What is the matter with the Pittsburg Stockman? In the issue of January 8, appears an editorial very disparaging to refrigerator beef and to those butchers who deal in it. It concludes: "Those butchers who give it a wide berth are evidently the wisest and most prosperous of their class." One of the editors and proprietors of our esteemed contemporary is a dealer in and a shipper of cattle on the hoof, but that fact should not bias the judgment of such a paper. Perhaps the view taken is from the standpoint of the near-by Pennsylvania feeders, and is in no sense a view as broad as the name of the paper, "National," would seem to suggest as being proper. The idea that western dressed beef is in any sense inferior in quality to that slaughtered on the spot is absurd. Some of the best cattle arriving at Chicago are killed and dressed here and sent east in refrigerator cars. Would the beef be better if the animals were shipped in uncomfortable stock cars 500 to 1,000 miles farther and slaughtered within a few blocks of where they are to be consumed?—[Drovers' Journal.
articles.summary: Clipped Drovers' Journal item defending refrigerator (dressed) beef against the Pittsburg Stockman.

articles.headline: Smiles. / The Dude and His Pop.
articles.text: [Not transcribed: clipped humor — the verse "Smiles" and two humorous sketches, the last headed "The Dude and His Pop" and credited to the Cincinnati Merchant Traveler.]
articles.summary: Clipped humorous verse and anecdotes (Smiles; The Dude and His Pop, from the Cincinnati Merchant Traveler); syndicated miscellany, not local news.

Ready-print page: Proceedings of Congress, Wellington anecdotes, fiction and miscellany, and patent-medicine and mail-order advertisements.

articles.text:
Bad Lands Cow Boy,
By A. T. Packard.

Thursday, Jan. 29, 1885.
articles.summary: Page 4 masthead.

articles.text: Rev. Father Martin was here Tuesday.
articles.summary: Father Martin visited.

articles.text: Northern Pacific preferred bonds are selling at 38⅝, and common at 16½.
articles.summary: N.P. bond prices.

articles.text: Abe Goodkind, of Wise & Goodkind, Bismarck, scattered a few of his mellifluous smiles among the boys Monday.
articles.summary: Abe Goodkind of Bismarck visited.

articles.text: D. O. Sweet and wife, of Buffalo Creek station, on the stage line, came up on last Friday's coach to visit the metropolis and lay in supplies.
articles.summary: D. O. Sweet and wife came in from Buffalo Creek station.

articles.text: Considerable difficulty has been experienced from snow on the stage line and sleds will be used as a relief on some of the routes until the snow melts.
articles.summary: Snow troubles on the stage line; sleds to be used.

articles.text: W. L. Hall, of the Vermont Cattle Co., was a passenger on Monday's coach. His ranch is on the South Moreau, about twenty miles from the stage crossing.
articles.summary: W. L. Hall of the Vermont Cattle Co. arrived by coach.

articles.text: Tom Jones has been in New York for some time and it is supposed that Joe. Pennell is now there. The mule outfit, with which the contract work on the Canadian Pacific was done, is at Port Arthur.
articles.summary: News of Tom Jones and Joe Pennell; their mule outfit at Port Arthur.

articles.text: Judge Bennett, of Deadwood, went down on Monday's coach. Ex-Sheriff Belding, who came up with him, still lingers in Bismarck, where he has been unanimously elected president of the third house.
articles.summary: Judge Bennett of Deadwood left on Monday's coach; ex-Sheriff Belding in Bismarck.

articles.text: W. B. Milne, who is doing a good business in Medora for his house, Wyman, Mullin & Van Dyke, of Minneapolis, was here Monday. He is always welcome and is one of the most popular travelling men on the road.
articles.summary: Travelling salesman W. B. Milne visited.

articles.text: George T. Reynolds, of Albany, Texas, intends putting in about eight thousand head of Texas steers a few miles down the river this summer. He is already making preparations, and will ship the cattle to Cheyenne or Valentine and drive the rest of the way.
articles.summary: George T. Reynolds plans to bring 8,000 Texas steers to the river.

articles.text: J. P. Elverson resigned some time ago as night operator at the depot and W. H. Minty of Minneapolis now takes his place. A. D. Green has been transferred to New Rockford and G. G. Cooper takes his place. Mr. Elverson will remain with us for some time.
articles.summary: Changes among the depot telegraph operators.

articles.text: The storm of Sunday and Monday was the deepest of the season, about four inches on a level. Considerable fear was expressed that cattle would suffer, but on the ranges, plenty of grass is showing above the snow and four more inches would not do much harm,
articles.summary: Sunday-Monday snowstorm, deepest of the season.

articles.text: The report that four of the Hash Knife cow boys have been frozen to death has been corroborated. They became bewildered in a storm, shot two of their ponies, went into camp and were frozen. There is also a report that three of the VVV boys were frozen, but it lacks confirmation.
articles.summary: Four Hash Knife cowboys reported frozen to death.

articles.text: Howard Eaton reports that while in St. Paul, the N. P., through an agent, definitely agreed to put in shipping yards here. This will be a great advantage to our Bad Lands cattle men as much difficulty has been experienced heretofore, owing to a lack of loading and unloading facilities.
articles.summary: N.P. agrees to build shipping yards at Medora.

articles.text: Bob Roberts started for Wales yesterday morning. He will stop off at Bismarck, St. Paul and Chicago several days, and in New York about a week. He will then go to Wales to settle his father's estate, and return to Medora in April. During his absence, Sam Townsend will have charge of his mule train.
articles.summary: Bob Roberts leaves for Wales to settle his father's estate.

articles.text: A postal from Levi Deffebach to Rassie, written just before the former's departure from New York to Germany, contains the welcome news that all necessary papers had been found, and that there was no difficulty feared in settling the estate very soon. Our readers will remember that a large fortune in Germany is awaiting the Deffebach heirs.
articles.summary: Levi Deffebach expects the German estate to be settled soon.

articles.text: Gregor Lang was in town Saturday and reports cattle at the Neimmela ranch as doing spledidly. The 7 7 7 and OX outfits are near him and loss is almost nothing. Mr. Lang only knows of three of his cattle dying, two killed by wolves and one by accident. There are probably other dead cattle but they are few and Mr. Lang estimates the loss in his neighborhood at less than one per cent.
articles.summary: Gregor Lang reports cattle at the Neimmela ranch doing well.

articles.text: The following are the arrivals and departures on the Medora Stage and Forwarding Co.'s line since our last issue: P. D. O'Brien and wife, C. E. Nichols, F. Schnieder, Thomas Leroy, William Penhall, William Angove, Joseph Austin, J. H. Williams, Mrs. J. H. Williams, S. C. Butcher, S. P. Smith, W. H. Lindenbaum, Etta Lindenbaum, William Brown, F. T. Flannigan, John Calahan. Departures: Judge Bennett, W. L. Hall.
articles.summary: Stage line arrivals and departures for the week.

articles.text: "'Twas ever thus." There was an attempt to organize an operatic troupe here, but it broke up on the first rehearsal. The affecting ditty, "Dem Golden Slippers" was being sung. The basso-profundo attempted to ring in the tune to the doxology, the tenor was singing—well it must have been the tune the old cow died of, and the chorus consisted of "Oh, cheese it," "Hit 'em with a club," and the Alaskan echo of "The psalm-singin' [sackers?] must be abated, dead or alive."
articles.summary: A Medora operatic troupe broke up at its first rehearsal.

articles.text: Thomas Brydon, who has been clerking for Arch. Boyd, left this morning for Mandan.
articles.summary: Thomas Brydon left for Mandan.

articles.text: As soon as Joe O'Brien returns, Dan. McKenzie will take a vacation and visit relatives in the east.
articles.summary: Dan McKenzie plans an eastern vacation.

articles.text: Windy Bill and Dutch Bill were in town this week, enlightening the pilgrims as to how to run a "stage wagon."
articles.summary: Windy Bill and Dutch Bill in town.

articles.text: All stockmen should bear in mind the annual meeting of the Little Missouri Association in April, and be prepared to make it a profitable one.
articles.summary: Reminder of the Little Missouri stock association's April annual meeting.

articles.text: The last ice house is about two-thirds full and a week more will probably see the ice crop harvested. There will be a total of six thousand tons, put up here.
articles.summary: Ice harvest nearly finished; 6,000 tons.

articles.text: Wallace Lozier, of New York, a friend of J. R. Grymes, is here visiting the latter. He will take up his residence in Medora, and doubtless make a good citizen.
articles.summary: Wallace Lozier of New York to settle in Medora.

articles.text: Johnny Goodall is in St. Paul and will return in a few days. Joe O'Brien will come with him. It's ten to one that Johnny don't wear the same head-gear here that he did in St. Paul.
articles.summary: Johnny Goodall in St. Paul.

articles.text: George Fitzgerald's new hotel is nearly completed, and it will probably be ready for occupancy next week. When completed, and the brick work finished in the spring, it will compare favorably with any hotel on the line.
articles.summary: George Fitzgerald's new hotel nearly finished.

articles.text: "Jim" Cook, whom our readers will remember as Studebaker's northwestern agent, has secured a far preferable position with the Walter A. Wood's firm, and writes that he is enjoying life as much as he always did while here.
articles.summary: Jim Cook takes a position with Walter A. Wood.

articles.text: Work on the slaughter house is progressing rapidly and only a part of the inside work remains to be done. It is built on the latest and most scientific principles and will do the work intended as well as any in the United States.
articles.summary: Medora slaughter house nearly complete.

articles.text: Mr. Edick, of Bismarck, made our cigar dealers a call Tuesday. His appearance everywhere is an "Emblem" of success. He, as well as all other traveling men, says that collections are better at Medora than at any point on the road.
articles.summary: Mr. Edick of Bismarck called on cigar dealers.

articles.text: Business is brisk on the stage line Eleven passengers came in last night, and several others who wanted to come were forced to remain over until the next coach. It will be hard work to accommodate all who want to come when the spring rush for Butte City and Coeur D'Alene begins.
articles.summary: Eleven stage passengers arrived; heavy traffic expected in spring.

articles.text: Howard Eaton returned from his eastern trip Sunday night. His leg has inproved considerably, but no operation was performed on it, as it might get well without and in any event it could as well be performed five years hence as now. Howard started for his Beaver creek ranch yesterday.
articles.summary: Howard Eaton back from the east, then off to his Beaver Creek ranch.

articles.text: Lloyd Roberts, than whom there is no one better prepared to speak on the subject, says that there are more yearlings and two-year-olds for sale in Minnesota and Iowa than ever before, and that they are also cheaper than ever. Mixed lots can easily be landed in Medora for less than twenty dollars a head.
articles.summary: Lloyd Roberts on cheap young cattle available from Minnesota and Iowa.

articles.text:
Alaska John broke out in a fresh place yesterday and the following sign now adorns the front of the "Oyster Grotto:"

FRESH OYSTERS, BLOOD RAW, DEAD OR ALIVE.

"Toosh."
articles.summary: Alaska John's new sign at the Oyster Grotto.

articles.text: A mistaken idea seems to be prevalent that we are not to have the freight shipped to the Hills via Medora this season, or that we will have to divide, as heretofore, with Dickinson and Belfield. We wish to make the statement right here that after July 22, 1885, every pound of freight shipped from the Northern Pacific into the the Hills will be shipped via Medora. A cast iron contract was drawn up some time ago between the Medora Stage and Forwarding Co. and the Northern Pacific, the terms of which are substantially as follows: That Dickinson, nor any other town on the Northern Pacific, shall have any other than regular local rates granted on shipments to the Hills, except Belfield. That as soon as the Belfield contract ran out, which will be July 22, 1885, Medora is to be the only town on the Northern Pacific that shall receive rates on Black Hills shipments. This contract is definite, and there is no question that Medora, after July, will receive all the benefit from the Black Hills trade. As every one knows, this alone will be enough to make a good town. Before this time, also, the Refrigerator company will be working on full time, all other industries tributary to Medora will be under full headway, and we are certain of having the liveliest, as we have heretofore had the best town for its size on the road.
articles.summary: After July 22, 1885, all Black Hills freight from the N.P. is to go via Medora under contract with the Medora Stage and Forwarding Co.

J. C. Fisher, Postmaster.
articles.summary: List of unclaimed letters at the Medora post office.

City Drug Store, Medora, Dak., H. M. Jorgens, Proprietor — drugs, patent medicines, perfumery, toilet articles, notions, periodicals, stationery
Franz Falk Brewing Co., Milwaukee, Wis. — Milwaukee Beer; Roberts & Co., Medora, agents; Otto Fisher, manager of Bismarck branch
E. J. Owenhouse, Bozeman, Mont. — stock saddles, Concord harness, fancy bits and spurs, chaparejos, reatas, quirts, hackamores
Mayville Stock Farm, Mayville, Traill Co., Dak. — Mayville herd of Short Horns, bulls for sale; W. W. Warner, general manager

Brand: Badger Cattle Company, Howard Eaton, Mgr., P.O. Medora — range Beaver creek and Little Missouri river
Brand: Dorr Clark, Spearfish, Dakota — V V V; range Belle Fourche

Brand: H. R. Tarbell & Co., Medora — horse brand; range Davis creek and Little Missouri
Brand: W. N. Thompson & Co., Wm. Dantz, Manager, P.O. Medora — TD and quarter-circle diamond

Brand: Custer Trail Cattle Co., F. Alden Eaton, Supt., P.O. Medora — HK and others; range Little Missouri, Deep and Davis creeks

articles.summary: Directory of display advertisements and cattle-brand advertisements in columns 3-8 of page 4.

events.date_basis: "To-day" in Thu 29 Jan 1885 issue (Vol. 1, No. 52)
events.title: The Bad Lands Cow Boy turns one year old
events.summary: The paper announced it was one year old and hoped to grow with its years.
events.excerpt: To-day, the Cow Boy is one year old. It is a pretty healthy infant

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 29 Jan 1885 issue
events.title: Bills to move the Dakota capital defeated
events.summary: The paper reported that the capital-removal bills in both houses of the territorial legislature had been defeated and that Bismarck would remain the capital.
events.excerpt: The bills for the removal of the capitol in both the house and council have been "gently but firmly squashed."

events.date_basis: "On and after the next issue" after Thu 29 Jan 1885; next weekly issue Thu 5 Feb 1885
events.title: Cow Boy cuts its brand-advertising rate to $15 a year
events.summary: The paper announced that from its next issue cattle-brand advertisements would cost $15 a year, to meet outside competition and draw every brand on the river.
events.excerpt: On and after the next issue of the Cow Boy the price of cattle brands will be reduced to $15 per year.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 29 Jan 1885 issue
events.title: Cow Boy urges quarantine against Texas fever
events.summary: The paper urged a quarantine for Texas cattle shipped into Dakota, perhaps on part of the Sioux reservation, and suggested the stock association meet before its April meeting.
events.excerpt: it might be a good plan to set off a portion of the Sioux reservation as a quarantine ground.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 29 Jan 1885 issue
events.title: Cow Boy opposes dividing Dakota
events.summary: In an editorial on admission and division, the paper favored admitting Dakota as a single state and blamed politicians for the division movement.
events.excerpt: we do not believe there is a private citizen of Dakota that way down in his heart wants our territory divided.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 29 Jan 1885 issue
events.title: Cow Boy calls for cowboys to leave six-shooters out of town
events.summary: The paper said Medora had never seen a six-shooter row among cowboys but joined other cattle papers in urging that six-shooters not be carried in town.
events.excerpt: Although Medora has never been the scene, in spite of all reports to the contrary, of a six-shooter row among cow boys

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 29 Jan 1885 issue
events.title: Coldest winter on record, but Bad Lands cattle thriving
events.summary: The paper reported the coldest winter ever known in the west and the deepest snow in years, but said cattle were in fine condition and Bad Lands losses would not exceed three per cent by spring.
events.excerpt: not over three per cent. of cattle will have died in the Bad Lands by spring

events.date_basis: "while here last summer" relative to Jan 1885
events.title: L. C. Le Moyne predicts Polled-Angus will rule the range
events.summary: The paper recalled that L. C. Le Moyne of the Le Moyne Cattle Co., while in Medora the previous summer, predicted Polled-Angus bulls would be the range favorites.
events.excerpt: while here last summer expressed his firm belief that Polled-Angus bulls would be the future favorites

events.date_basis: Notice gives "the night of November 19" (1884)
events.title: A. Young's mare strays from his ranch south of Medora
events.summary: A. Young advertised for a dark sorrel mare branded M bar, lost from his ranch ten miles south of Medora.
events.excerpt: From my ranch on Little Missouri, ten miles south of Medora, the night of November 19, a dark sorrel mare

events.date_basis: Notice gives "July 6, 1884"
events.title: John Pohl's horse lost on the Little Missouri
events.summary: A notice offered $25 for John Pohl's bay horse, branded with an anchor and hat brand, lost from Little Missouri.
events.excerpt: From Little Missouri, July 6, 1884, a bay horse

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 29 Jan 1885 issue
events.title: Gregor Lang offers $50 for missing horses
events.summary: Gregor Lang offered a $50 reward for three young mares and a sorrel pony carrying his advertised brands.
events.excerpt: The above reward will be paid for the return of the following stock

events.date_basis: "Tuesday" before Thu 29 Jan 1885
events.title: Father Martin visits Medora
events.summary: The paper noted that Rev. Father Martin was in town.
events.excerpt: Rev. Father Martin was here Tuesday.

events.date_basis: "Monday" before Thu 29 Jan 1885
events.title: Abe Goodkind of Bismarck visits
events.summary: Abe Goodkind of Wise & Goodkind, Bismarck, visited the town.
events.excerpt: scattered a few of his mellifluous smiles among the boys Monday.

events.date_basis: "last Friday's coach" before Thu 29 Jan 1885
events.title: D. O. Sweet and wife come up from Buffalo Creek station
events.summary: D. O. Sweet and his wife, of Buffalo Creek station on the stage line, came to Medora for supplies.
events.excerpt: came up on last Friday's coach to visit the metropolis and lay in supplies.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 29 Jan 1885 issue
events.title: Snow hampers the Black Hills stage line
events.summary: Snow caused difficulty on the stage line and sleds were to be used on some routes until it melted.
events.excerpt: sleds will be used as a relief on some of the routes until the snow melts.

events.date_basis: "Monday's coach" before Thu 29 Jan 1885
events.title: W. L. Hall of the Vermont Cattle Co. travels by stage
events.summary: W. L. Hall, whose ranch is on the South Moreau, was a passenger on Monday's coach; he is listed among the week's departures.
events.excerpt: W. L. Hall, of the Vermont Cattle Co., was a passenger on Monday's coach.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 29 Jan 1885 issue
events.title: Tom Jones and Joe Pennell in New York
events.summary: Tom Jones had been in New York and Joe Pennell was supposed to be there; their mule outfit from the Canadian Pacific contract was at Port Arthur.
events.excerpt: The mule outfit, with which the contract work on the Canadian Pacific was done, is at Port Arthur.

events.date_basis: "Monday's coach" before Thu 29 Jan 1885
events.title: Judge Bennett of Deadwood leaves on the coach
events.summary: Judge Bennett of Deadwood went down on Monday's coach; ex-Sheriff Belding stayed in Bismarck, where he was elected president of the "third house."
events.excerpt: Judge Bennett, of Deadwood, went down on Monday's coach.

events.date_basis: "Monday" before Thu 29 Jan 1885
events.title: Salesman W. B. Milne visits Medora
events.summary: W. B. Milne of Wyman, Mullin & Van Dyke, Minneapolis, called in Medora.
events.excerpt: W. B. Milne, who is doing a good business in Medora for his house

events.date_basis: "this summer" relative to Jan 1885
events.title: George T. Reynolds plans to bring 8,000 Texas steers to the Little Missouri
events.summary: George T. Reynolds of Albany, Texas, planned to put about 8,000 Texas steers a few miles down the river, shipping them to Cheyenne or Valentine and driving the rest.
events.excerpt: intends putting in about eight thousand head of Texas steers a few miles down the river this summer.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 29 Jan 1885 issue
events.title: Changes among Medora's depot operators
events.summary: W. H. Minty of Minneapolis replaced J. P. Elverson as night operator at the depot; A. D. Green was transferred to New Rockford and replaced by G. G. Cooper.
events.excerpt: W. H. Minty of Minneapolis now takes his place.

events.date_basis: "Sunday and Monday" before Thu 29 Jan 1885
events.title: Deepest snowstorm of the season
events.summary: The Sunday-Monday storm left about four inches of snow, the deepest of the season, but grass still showed above it on the ranges.
events.excerpt: The storm of Sunday and Monday was the deepest of the season, about four inches on a level.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 29 Jan 1885 issue
events.title: Four Hash Knife cowboys frozen to death
events.summary: The paper reported confirmation that four Hash Knife cowboys froze to death after becoming lost in a storm; a report that three VVV hands also froze was unconfirmed.
events.excerpt: The report that four of the Hash Knife cow boys have been frozen to death has been corroborated.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 29 Jan 1885 issue
events.title: Northern Pacific agrees to build shipping yards at Medora
events.summary: Howard Eaton reported that the Northern Pacific had agreed in St. Paul to put in cattle shipping yards at Medora.
events.excerpt: the N. P., through an agent, definitely agreed to put in shipping yards here.

events.date_basis: "yesterday morning" before Thu 29 Jan 1885
events.title: Bob Roberts leaves for Wales
events.summary: Bob Roberts left for Wales to settle his father's estate, planning to return in April; Sam Townsend took charge of his mule train.
events.excerpt: Bob Roberts started for Wales yesterday morning.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 29 Jan 1885 issue
events.title: Deffebach heirs near settlement of German estate
events.summary: A postal card from Levi Deffebach to Rassie said the papers for the family's German inheritance had been found and the estate should be settled soon.
events.excerpt: a large fortune in Germany is awaiting the Deffebach heirs.

events.date_basis: "Saturday" before Thu 29 Jan 1885
events.title: Gregor Lang reports Neimmela cattle doing well
events.summary: Gregor Lang, in town, said cattle at the Neimmela ranch were doing well, with only three losses, two to wolves.
events.excerpt: reports cattle at the Neimmela ranch as doing spledidly.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 29 Jan 1885 issue
events.title: Stage arrivals and departures
events.summary: The paper listed sixteen arrivals on the Medora Stage and Forwarding Co. line since the last issue and the departures of Judge Bennett and W. L. Hall.
events.excerpt: The following are the arrivals and departures on the Medora Stage and Forwarding Co.'s line since our last issue

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 29 Jan 1885 issue
events.title: Medora operatic troupe breaks up at first rehearsal
events.summary: An attempt to organize an operatic troupe in Medora broke up at its first rehearsal of "Dem Golden Slippers."
events.excerpt: There was an attempt to organize an operatic troupe here, but it broke up on the first rehearsal.

events.date_basis: "this morning" in Thu 29 Jan 1885 issue
events.title: Thomas Brydon leaves for Mandan
events.summary: Thomas Brydon, clerk for Arch. Boyd, left for Mandan.
events.excerpt: Thomas Brydon, who has been clerking for Arch. Boyd, left this morning for Mandan.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 29 Jan 1885 issue
events.title: Dan McKenzie plans a trip east
events.summary: Dan McKenzie was to take a vacation in the east once Joe O'Brien returned.
events.excerpt: Dan. McKenzie will take a vacation and visit relatives in the east.

events.date_basis: "in April"; annual meeting
events.title: Little Missouri stock association to hold annual meeting in April
events.summary: The paper reminded stockmen of the Little Missouri association's annual meeting in April.
events.excerpt: the annual meeting of the Little Missouri Association in April

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 29 Jan 1885 issue
events.title: Medora ice harvest nearly finished
events.summary: The last ice house was two-thirds full and the harvest, totalling 6,000 tons, was expected to finish within a week.
events.excerpt: There will be a total of six thousand tons, put up here.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 29 Jan 1885 issue
events.title: Wallace Lozier of New York to settle in Medora
events.summary: Wallace Lozier, a friend of J. R. Grymes, was visiting and planned to make Medora his home.
events.excerpt: He will take up his residence in Medora

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 29 Jan 1885 issue
events.title: George Fitzgerald's hotel nearly complete
events.summary: George Fitzgerald's new hotel was nearly finished and expected to open the next week, with brick work to follow in spring.
events.excerpt: George Fitzgerald's new hotel is nearly completed

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 29 Jan 1885 issue
events.title: Medora slaughter house nearly complete
events.summary: Work on the slaughter house was progressing rapidly, with only part of the inside work left.
events.excerpt: Work on the slaughter house is progressing rapidly

events.date_basis: "Tuesday" before Thu 29 Jan 1885
events.title: Mr. Edick of Bismarck calls on Medora cigar dealers
events.summary: Mr. Edick of Bismarck visited; travelling men said collections were better in Medora than anywhere on the road.
events.excerpt: collections are better at Medora than at any point on the road.

events.date_basis: "last night" relative to Thu 29 Jan 1885
events.title: Eleven passengers arrive on the stage
events.summary: Eleven passengers arrived by stage and others had to wait for the next coach; a spring rush to Butte City and Coeur d'Alene was expected.
events.excerpt: Eleven passengers came in last night

events.date_basis: "Sunday night" before Thu 29 Jan 1885
events.title: Howard Eaton returns from the east
events.summary: Howard Eaton returned from his eastern trip, his leg improved without an operation, and left for his Beaver Creek ranch on the 28th.
events.excerpt: Howard Eaton returned from his eastern trip Sunday night.

events.date_basis: "yesterday" before Thu 29 Jan 1885
events.title: Alaska John puts up a new sign at the Oyster Grotto
events.summary: Alaska John hung a sign at the Oyster Grotto advertising fresh oysters "blood raw, dead or alive."
events.excerpt: FRESH OYSTERS, BLOOD RAW, DEAD OR ALIVE.

events.date_basis: Text gives "after July 22, 1885"
events.title: All Black Hills freight to go via Medora
events.summary: The paper said a contract between the Medora Stage and Forwarding Co. and the Northern Pacific would make Medora the only N.P. town with Black Hills freight rates once Belfield's contract expired July 22, 1885.
events.excerpt: after July 22, 1885, every pound of freight shipped from the Northern Pacific into the the Hills will be shipped via Medora.
